description:
Wesam Saad brings the discussion of creation’s restoration to a close by examining passages that describe heaven and earth passing away. He asks whether the language of destruction requires the disappearance of creation itself. Reading 2 Peter 3 alongside its account of the flood, he argues that judgment can devastate the earth without annihilating it. Fire, in this reading, prepares the way for renewal.

The study compares this language with the believer becoming a new creation and with creation’s expectation of freedom in Romans 8. Saad distinguishes transformed desires from the replacement of a person’s identity, then applies that distinction to the promised earth. Acts 3 supplies the language of restoration. He also distinguishes restoring God’s good creation from simply returning humanity to a garden occupied by two people; God’s purpose for a populated earth remains in view.

The practical concern is trust in God’s character. Saad presents restoration as an expression of divine power, care and faithfulness. A future connected with familiar creation, freed from its curse, gives believers something concrete to anticipate. That hope, he argues, strengthens their willingness to make present sacrifices for Christ.

questions.question: Why does Saad read the destruction in 2 Peter 3 alongside the flood?
questions.answer: Peter first describes the earlier world as destroyed by water. Saad points out that creation continued after that judgment, even though lives and the earth’s condition were profoundly affected. He therefore argues that the later language of fiery destruction need not mean the complete annihilation of creation.

questions.question: How does becoming a new creation help explain the earth’s renewal?
questions.answer: Saad compares the earth passing away with the old passing away when someone comes to Christ. The believer remains the same person, while desires, relationships and standing in Christ change. He uses this continuity of identity to argue that making something new does not necessarily mean replacing its existence.

questions.question: What does creation’s hope in Romans 8 contribute to the argument?
questions.answer: Creation is pictured as awaiting release from corruption, not wishing to cease existing. Saad treats this longing as figurative language that expresses the promise of liberation. In his explanation, being set free means that the creation already present is transformed rather than discarded.

questions.question: How does Saad distinguish restoration from returning to only Adam and Eve in a garden?
questions.answer: He includes the earth, living creatures and righteous humanity within restoration, while recognising God’s command to fill the earth. The creation’s original goodness does not require permanently limiting it to two people. Cities and other forms of human organisation are discussed as possible expressions of a populated earth, not as the problem that redemption must remove.

questions.question: What does the promised restoration reveal about God in this study?
questions.answer: Saad argues that restoring what sin has corrupted displays God’s power, faithfulness, care and skill. He presents redemption of the whole creation as the completion of God’s victory, rather than a concession that the original creation cannot be recovered. These conclusions are his explanation of why the distinction matters.

questions.question: How can a renewed earth strengthen present commitment to Christ?
questions.answer: Saad asks listeners to imagine familiar creation without its curse, thorns and fruitlessness. He says this gives hope a concrete object rather than an entirely foreign future. Anticipating that promised world can deepen the conviction that present sacrifices made for Christ are worthwhile.

questions.question: Does the session settle every question about the sea, sun and moon?
questions.answer: No. Saad says that the question about the sea requires further discussion. He argues that the New Jerusalem having no need of the sun does not itself prove that the sun will not exist, using the difference between an overshadowed light and an absent one. The study preserves that distinction without presenting a complete account of these details.
